Adding a language does not always add its keyboard. On iOS you add layouts under General, in the Keyboards list, then switch with the globe key. Android installs input methods per keyboard app, so a Gboard user adds languages inside Gboard rather than in system settings alone.

Windows attaches keyboard layouts to each installed language and exposes them in the taskbar language switcher, which is why a UK layout can appear on a US install and swap the quote and at symbols. Ubuntu and ChromeOS both list input sources separately from display language for the same reason. If you write in two scripts daily, add both layouts once and leave them installed.

body.h2: Region controls dates, currency and units
body.html:
Region format is a formatting engine, not a translation. It drives the first day of the week, 12 or 24-hour clock, temperature units, paper size, decimal separator and the currency symbol that apps inherit by default.

Because it is inherited, a spreadsheet opened on a machine with a comma decimal separator can misread numbers exported from a machine using a full stop. Setting region explicitly on both, rather than relying on the language default, prevents that. Windows also separates the regional format from the display language, so you can run an English interface with German formatting. Comparing how the two families organise this is one of the clearer differences in the iOS versus Android comparison.

You no longer have to change the whole system for one app. iOS 13 and later expose a Language entry inside each app's own settings page, and Android 13 added App languages under the system Languages screen. macOS offers the same per-app override in its Language and Region pane.

Switching to Arabic, Hebrew, Farsi or Urdu also mirrors the interface: navigation bars, back arrows and list alignment flip to right-to-left, and some apps need a restart to redraw correctly. Assistants are separate again, with Siri and Google Assistant keeping their own language setting. Use the settings finder when a menu has moved, browse the Ubuntu hub for the desktop layout, and try the changes first in the settings simulator so you can always find your way back.

faq.q: Why is my device still showing English after changing the language?
faq.a: Apps only translate into languages their developers shipped. If an app has no translation for your choice, it falls back to the next language in your list, usually English.

faq.q: Can I use one language for the interface and another for formatting?
faq.a: Yes. Windows, macOS, Ubuntu and ChromeOS all separate display language from regional format, and iOS lets you set region independently of language.

faq.q: How do I get my old language back if the menus are unreadable?
faq.a: The language pane sits in the same position regardless of language, so count the rows to reach it. On Windows you can also switch back from the taskbar language button.

key: Language sets menu text; region sets dates, units and currency
Keyboards are added separately from the display language
iOS 13+ and Android 13+ both support per-app language overrides

title: Accessibility Settings on Every OS: iOS, Android, Windows, Mac
h1: The accessibility settings worth knowing on every operating system
desc: Find the accessibility settings that matter on iOS, Android, macOS, Windows, ChromeOS and Ubuntu: screen readers, text size, reduce motion and captions.
lede: Six major operating systems keep their accessibility tools in a section with almost the same name, but the labels underneath drift apart. Here is what each platform calls the features you are most likely to need, and where the wording changes between versions.

body.html:
Every mainstream operating system now gathers its accessibility tools in one place, and the name has converged on Accessibility. On iOS and iPadOS the section sits at the top level of Settings from iOS 13 onwards; on older releases it lived inside General, which still catches people following out-of-date instructions.

Windows 11 renamed the Windows 10 Ease of Access section to Accessibility, macOS moved its pane into the redesigned System Settings sidebar in Ventura, and the GNOME desktop that Ubuntu ships replaced the old Universal Access label with Accessibility. The features barely changed. The doors moved.

Screen readers are the deepest feature in the list and each platform ships its own. iOS and macOS use VoiceOver, Android uses TalkBack, Windows uses Narrator, ChromeOS uses ChromeVox and Ubuntu uses Orca.

All of them can be switched on from the Accessibility section, and all of them have a keyboard or button shortcut that toggles them again. Learn the off switch before you turn one on, because the interface changes immediately. Reading iOS compared with Android makes the naming differences easier to keep straight.

body.h2: Text size, bold text and zoom
body.html:
Text size is the setting most people actually want. iOS offers Larger Text and Bold Text under Display and Text Size, Android exposes separate font size and display size controls, and Windows 11 has a system-wide text size slider that scales apps without touching the screen resolution.

macOS leans on display scaling and per-app text options rather than one global slider, while Ubuntu offers a large text switch alongside a cursor size control. ChromeOS pairs a font size setting with a full-screen magnifier, and the ChromeOS settings hub shows where those sit next to the display options.

body.h2: Reduce motion, contrast and colour filters
body.html:
Reduce Motion removes the zooming and sliding animations that trigger nausea for some people and simply waste time for everyone else. Apple uses that exact name, Windows 11 groups it under visual effects as animation effects, GNOME calls it reduce animation, and recent Android versions offer a remove animations toggle whose label depends on the manufacturer's skin.

Colour filters exist on all six systems, usually with presets for the common forms of colour vision deficiency. Contrast is a separate control, so if text is still hard to read after a filter, look for high contrast or contrast themes as well.

body.h2: Captions, switch control and voice control
body.html:
Caption settings do not create captions; they style them. You choose font, size and background for subtitles that apps render through the system, under a name like subtitles and captioning or caption preferences. Android's live caption is the exception, because it generates captions on the device for almost any audio.

Switch Control on Apple systems and Switch Access on Android let external buttons drive the whole interface, while voice control and voice access do the same with speech. Both are easy to enable by accident, so practise the exit route first.

body.h2: Finding the right menu without a spare device
body.html:
Because labels move between versions, the fastest way to help someone is to open the same menu they are looking at. The settings finder searches paths by name across systems, and the version change log records what was renamed between releases.

You can walk the real accessibility trees for iOS, Android, Windows, macOS, ChromeOS and Ubuntu in the osimulator settings simulator, then follow the language and region guide if a device is showing its menus in a language you cannot read.

faq.q: Where is Accessibility on iPhone?
faq.a: It is a top-level entry in Settings on iOS 13 and later. On iOS 12 and earlier it sits inside Settings, General, Accessibility.

faq.q: What replaced Ease of Access in Windows?
faq.a: Windows 11 renamed the section to Accessibility and reorganised it into vision, hearing and interaction groups. The individual features carried over from Windows 10.

faq.q: Do accessibility settings sync between devices?
faq.a: Some do within one ecosystem, such as Apple devices sharing certain preferences over iCloud, but most are per device. Assume you need to set each device separately.

key: Accessibility is now the section name on all six major systems
Screen readers: VoiceOver, TalkBack, Narrator, ChromeVox, Orca
Learn the off shortcut before enabling a screen reader

title: ChromeOS vs Ubuntu: Which Simple Desktop Actually Suits You?
h1: ChromeOS vs Ubuntu for beginners
desc: ChromeOS vs Ubuntu for beginners: how each handles updates, apps, files, printing and privacy, plus an honest look at who each desktop actually suits.
lede: Both promise a desktop that stays out of your way, and both are cheap or free to run. They reach that goal from opposite directions, and the right choice depends almost entirely on what you do offline.

body.html:
ChromeOS is simple by subtraction. The browser is the computer, the settings list is short, and anything the system does not support is simply absent rather than hidden. Its Settings app groups options into Network, Bluetooth, Connected devices, Accounts, Device, Personalisation, Apps, Accessibility, Security and Privacy, and system preferences.

Ubuntu is simple by presentation. Underneath sits a full Linux system, but the GNOME Settings app shows a friendly sidebar of Wi-Fi, Network, Appearance, Notifications, Power, Displays, Printers, Users, Region & Language and Accessibility.

Ubuntu 24.04 reorganised several of those into a combined System section, so older screenshots do not always match. Both structures are machine-extracted for our simulator, as explained on the data provenance page.

ChromeOS updates itself in the background and applies the change on the next restart. You get an automatic update expiry date tied to the hardware model, after which that Chromebook stops receiving new versions, so check that date before buying second-hand.

Ubuntu prompts you instead. The Software Updater offers security and package updates, and long-term support releases arrive every two years with several years of maintenance. You choose when a major version upgrade happens.

The trade is control against effort, and the software update guide covers the mechanics on both.

App availability is the decision point. ChromeOS runs web apps natively, many Android apps on supported models, and optionally a Linux container for developer tools. Ubuntu runs native Linux applications installed from its App Center, from Snap or Flatpak packages, or from the command line.

Neither runs Windows or macOS software directly, so if you depend on a specific desktop application, check it works before switching.

  • Files: ChromeOS leans on Google Drive with a small local Downloads folder. Ubuntu treats local storage as the default and adds cloud accounts optionally.
  • Printing: both use the same driverless standards, so a modern network printer usually appears on its own. Older USB-only printers are more likely to work on Ubuntu, where manufacturer drivers can be installed.
  • Networking: both are straightforward, as shown in the Wi-Fi guide.

ChromeOS is built around a Google account. Sign-in, sync, backup and most personalisation flow through it, and while guest mode and local browsing exist, the account is the normal path. Verified boot and automatic updates make it hard to compromise, but the trade-off is that your profile lives with Google.

Ubuntu asks for no online account at all. You create a local user during installation and can decline every optional service, including telemetry. That independence comes with responsibility: you decide what to install and what to trust.

Language and region handling is broadly similar on both, and the change language guide covers the general route.

Choose ChromeOS if the computer is mainly for browsing, email, documents, video and school work, if someone else may need to support it remotely, or if you want a machine that essentially maintains itself.

Choose Ubuntu if you want offline applications, real file management, development tools, or a way to keep older hardware useful for years. It also suits anyone who prefers not to tie a desktop to a single company's account.

If you are weighing Ubuntu against a Mac instead, the macOS vs Ubuntu comparison is the closer match. Otherwise, open the real menus for ChromeOS and Ubuntu and click through them in the free browser simulator before you commit.

faq.q: Can I install Ubuntu on a Chromebook?
faq.a: On many models yes, either alongside ChromeOS in developer mode or as a full replacement, though the process varies by hardware and can void support. The built-in Linux container is a safer middle ground.

faq.q: Which is better for an older laptop?
faq.a: Ubuntu, in most cases. It installs on standard PC hardware and lightweight variants run well on modest specifications, whereas ChromeOS is designed to ship with the machine.

faq.q: Does Ubuntu need an internet connection to be useful?
faq.a: No. Ubuntu installs applications locally and works fully offline, while ChromeOS depends far more on a connection for its core web-based workflow.

key: ChromeOS updates itself; Ubuntu updates when you decide.
ChromeOS assumes a Google account, Ubuntu needs no account at all.
Pick ChromeOS for browsing, Ubuntu for offline apps and old hardware.

title: watchOS vs Wear OS: Settings on the Watch and on the Phone
h1: watchOS vs Wear OS settings, compared
desc: watchOS vs Wear OS compared: what you can change on the watch, what needs the phone app, and how faces, notifications, workouts and battery modes differ.
lede: Every smartwatch splits its settings between a tiny screen and a companion phone app. Apple and Google draw that line in noticeably different places.

body.h2: The split between watch and phone
body.html:
An Apple Watch has a Settings app on the wrist covering General, Display & Brightness, Sounds & Haptics, Focus, Passcode, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and Battery. The Watch app on a paired iPhone mirrors most of that and adds the parts that are painful on a small screen, such as app installation and face arrangement.

Wear OS works the same way in outline, with an on-watch Settings app and a companion on the phone. Which companion you get depends on the hardware: a Google Pixel Watch uses the Google Pixel Watch app, while Samsung devices use Galaxy Wearable.

That is the first real asymmetry. watchOS has one companion app for every model, Wear OS has several. The watchOS vs Wear OS comparison lays out both trees.

On watchOS you can add and edit a face directly on the watch by pressing and holding the current one, then choosing Edit to swap complications. The iPhone Watch app also carries a Face Gallery, which is the easier way to browse a large collection.

Wear OS uses the same two routes: press and hold the face on the watch to customise it, or use the phone app to browse and install faces. Google's newer Watch Face Format changed how third-party faces are built, so what you can tweak varies by face rather than by watch.

The vocabulary differs slightly too. Apple calls the small data widgets on a face complications; Wear OS uses complications on faces but also has Tiles, which are separate swipeable panels alongside the face.

Both platforms default to mirroring the phone. On watchOS, the Watch app's Notifications screen lets you keep Mirror my iPhone for most apps and set custom behaviour for Apple's own apps.

Wear OS mirrors phone notifications too, and you can block an app from the watch itself or from the companion app. Because Android already has per-channel notification controls, muting a channel on the phone usually mutes it on the watch as well.

If your wrist is buzzing constantly, the fix is normally upstream on the phone rather than on the watch, which the notifications guide covers.

watchOS keeps workout preferences in the Workout app settings on the watch, including auto-pause and end-of-workout reminders, while long-term health data lives in the Health app on the iPhone.

Wear OS depends on which health platform the watch ships with. Pixel Watch models route activity data through Fitbit, Samsung watches through Samsung Health, and each supplies its own goals and reminders screens.

Battery modes also diverge. Apple added a system-wide Low Power Mode in watchOS 9 that disables background heart rate readings and the always-on display. Wear OS offers Battery Saver plus vendor extras such as Samsung's watch-only mode. Either way, the always-on display is usually the single largest drain, as the battery life guide explains.

watchOS is the tidier system because it targets one phone platform and one manufacturer. Any Apple Watch tutorial applies to any Apple Watch of that version.

Wear OS is more flexible and more variable. It works across many Android phones and several watch makers, but menu names and companion apps shift between brands, so generic instructions fail more often.

Both start with the same step, pairing over Bluetooth, which the pairing guide covers. To see the actual menus before you buy, open watchOS and Wear OS in the free browser simulator and scroll through them.

faq.q: Can an Apple Watch pair with an Android phone?
faq.a: No. watchOS requires an iPhone for setup and for the companion Watch app, and there is no supported way to pair it with Android.

faq.q: Do I need the phone app to change watch settings?
faq.a: Not for most things. Both platforms expose display, sound, passcode and battery options on the watch itself, but app installation, face libraries and detailed notification rules are easier or only available on the phone.

faq.q: What is the difference between complications and Tiles?
faq.a: Complications are small data elements placed on the watch face itself, on both platforms. Tiles are Wear OS panels you swipe to beside the face, and they have no direct watchOS equivalent.

key: Both split settings between the watch and a companion phone app.
watchOS has one companion app; Wear OS varies by manufacturer.
Always-on display is the main battery drain on either platform.

title: PlayStation vs Xbox Settings: The Two Console Menus Compared
h1: PlayStation vs Xbox settings, menu by menu
desc: PlayStation vs Xbox settings compared: accounts and family, storage, HDR and video output, accessibility, power modes and network menus on both consoles.
lede: Sony and Microsoft solve the same problems with very different menu trees. Knowing which top-level heading owns a feature saves most of the hunting.

body.html:
On a PlayStation 5 the entry point is the gear icon in the top right of the home screen, which opens a long vertical list: Users and Accounts, Family and Parental Controls, Storage, Screen and Video, Sound, Accessibility, System, Network, and more.

On an Xbox Series X or S you press the Xbox button, move to Profile & system and choose Settings. The list is shorter because Microsoft groups aggressively: Account, General, Devices & connections, System, and Accessibility.

That grouping is the core difference. Sony gives many features their own top-level row, while Microsoft buries several inside General, including audio, display, power and network. The PlayStation vs Xbox comparison shows both trees together.

PlayStation splits this in two. Users and Accounts handles sign-in, linked services and account switching, while Family and Parental Controls is a separate top-level entry for child accounts, spending limits and playtime.

Xbox keeps sign-in and privacy under Account, and files child settings under General, then Online safety & family. Microsoft also pushes much of this to the web and to the Family Safety mobile app, so some limits are set off-console entirely.

Both let you require a passcode or password at sign-in, which is the single most useful change on a shared console, along the lines described in the lock and security guide.

Storage is a top-level PS5 item covering internal storage, an installed M.2 SSD and USB extended storage. Xbox files it under System, then Storage, covering internal, the proprietary expansion card and USB drives.

The rules are similar in spirit: current-generation titles need fast internal or expansion storage to run, while older-generation games can be played from a USB drive. Either way, clearing space is a recurring chore, and the storage guide covers the general approach.

For picture quality, PS5 uses Screen and Video, which holds resolution, HDR and a guided HDR adjustment. Xbox uses General, then TV & display options, which holds resolution, video modes and separate calibration tools for HDR games.

Accessibility is top-level on both, which is unusual and welcome. Each offers a screen reader, text size and contrast options, subtitle controls and controller button remapping.

Power differs in naming. PS5 groups rest mode behaviour and standby power under System, controlling whether the console keeps USB ports powered and downloads running. Xbox puts its power modes under General, then Power options, where the choice is essentially between fast resume and lower standby draw.

Network is top-level on PS5 and sits under General on Xbox. Both offer wired and wireless setup plus a connection test that reports NAT type, and the general steps match the Wi-Fi guide.

body.h2: Which menu is easier to navigate
body.html:
PlayStation is faster to scan. Because Storage, Network, Accessibility and Family each have their own row, you rarely need to guess where something was filed.

Xbox is tidier but requires more knowledge. Once you learn that General is the catch-all for audio, display, power and network, the tree becomes predictable, and Microsoft's search in the guide helps.

Neither is obviously better, and both change layout between system updates, so check your own dashboard version before following any tutorial. You can browse the actual menu structures for PlayStation and Xbox in the free browser simulator without a console in front of you.

faq.q: Can I play current-generation games from a USB drive?
faq.a: Generally no. Both consoles allow current-generation titles to be stored on USB for transfer, but they must be moved back to internal or expansion storage to run. Older-generation titles can usually run from USB.

faq.q: Where are HDR settings on each console?
faq.a: PlayStation keeps them under Screen and Video, including a step-by-step HDR adjustment. Xbox keeps them under General, then TV and display options, with separate calibration for HDR games.

faq.q: Which console has better parental controls?
faq.a: Both are capable. PlayStation puts Family and Parental Controls at the top level of the console menu, while Xbox splits controls between the console and Microsoft Family Safety on the web and mobile.

key: PlayStation gives most features a top-level row; Xbox nests them under General.
HDR lives in Screen and Video on PS5, TV and display options on Xbox.
Accessibility is a top-level menu on both consoles.

title: What Is a Settings Menu? How Every OS Stores Your Preferences
h1: What a settings menu actually is under the hood
desc: What is a settings menu really? A front end over preference stores, layered defaults and per-app scopes, and why every operating system grows a similar tree.
lede: A settings menu is not a list of switches; it is a view over a preference database. Understanding the store beneath it explains greyed-out toggles, resets and why every platform looks familiar.

body.h2: A settings menu is a view over a store
body.html:
Your choices do not live in the menu. The menu is a front end over one or more preference stores, and the tree you tap through is a presentation layer that a designer can rearrange without moving a single stored value.

The stores differ by platform. Apple systems use property lists read and written through the defaults system. Android keeps per-app preference files alongside system tables served by a settings provider. Windows writes to the registry. GNOME desktops such as Ubuntu use a binary dconf database described by GSettings schema files.

Every store works in layers. A shipped default sits underneath, your change sits on top of it, and in managed environments a policy or MDM profile can sit above both and win. That layering is why a reset can return a device to a known state rather than erasing it.

It also explains greyed-out toggles. A control that will not move usually has a value written above your layer, either by an administrator or by another setting that makes it meaningless. Clearing your layer so the defaults show through is what a device reset largely does.

Preferences split into system scope and user scope. System scope describes the machine: disk encryption, network interfaces, installed updates, which accounts may sign in. User scope describes one account: wallpaper, language, keyboard layout, notification choices.

The split is why some rows carry a padlock or demand a password, and why changing your display language need not change the login screen. Multi-user systems keep the two apart deliberately, and phones blur the line without removing it.

Per-app scoping gives each application its own namespace, so two apps can both store a key called theme without colliding. The operating system attaches its own per-app records too: granted permissions, notification rules, background activity, storage use and default-handler status.

That is why an app settings page usually mixes options the developer wrote with switches the system added. Removing the app removes its namespace, which is part of why uninstalling reliably frees storage and revokes permissions in one step.

body.h2: Why every OS grows a similar tree
body.html:
Different vendors converge on similar trees, and it is not simple copying. Every device has radios, a screen, sound, power, storage, an account, installed software, a language and a lock. Group those concerns sensibly and you land on roughly the same dozen sections whatever the platform.

The real differences are naming and depth. Android says Network & internet where iOS lists Wi-Fi and Bluetooth as separate rows; Windows says Personalization where macOS says Appearance. Section-by-section reading is why the comparison pages are laid out the way they are.

body.h2: Open-source systems let you read the tree
body.html:
Closed systems make you infer the hierarchy by tapping. Open ones publish it: Android ships its settings hierarchy as source, GNOME publishes schema files, and projects such as webOS OSE and the old Firefox OS interface expose their menus in the repository.

That makes the structure verifiable rather than approximate. The data provenance page records which trees were machine-extracted and which were rebuilt by hand, the changes log tracks version-to-version movement, and you can open the settings simulator to compare dozens of systems side by side.

faq.q: Why can I not change some settings?
faq.a: A policy, MDM profile or administrator account can write a value above yours, and the interface greys the control out rather than letting your change be silently ignored.

faq.q: Does a factory reset delete my settings?
faq.a: It clears your layer so the shipped defaults apply again. On most systems it also removes user data, which is a separate step from the preference reset itself.

faq.q: Why do menu paths change between versions?
faq.a: The tree is only a presentation layer. Vendors regroup and rename sections between releases while the underlying stored keys often stay the same.

key: The menu is a view; your choices live in a preference store.
Layered defaults, user values and policy explain greyed-out toggles.
Open-source systems publish their settings tree so it can be verified.

title: How OS Settings Menus Changed: From Control Panel to Search
h1: How settings menus changed, from icon grids to searchable sidebars
desc: See how settings menus changed from Mac OS X System Preferences and Windows Control Panel to searchable sidebars, and how to track renames version by version.
lede: Settings used to be a grid of icons you could learn by muscle memory. Two decades of new features, per-app permissions and touchscreens turned that grid into a searchable sidebar that changes names with almost every release.

body.html:
For twenty years, configuring a computer meant a grid of icons. Mac OS X shipped System Preferences in 2001 as rows of labelled squares, and Windows offered Control Panel, which by the Windows XP and Windows 7 era had grown a category view layered over an alphabetical list of applets.

The grid worked because there were only a few dozen things to configure. You learned where an icon sat and reached for it without reading. The Mac OS X hub and the Windows 7 hub preserve both layouts, and revisiting them shows how much smaller the configuration surface used to be.

Touchscreens broke the grid. Windows 8 introduced a separate PC settings app for the new interface while leaving Control Panel in place for everything the new app could not do yet, and Windows 10 continued the split with a Settings app that absorbed applets release by release.

That transition took roughly a decade, and it is not finished. Windows 11 still ships Control Panel, and certain dialogs around printers and regional formats hand you back to the older interface. Apple made a cleaner break: System Preferences kept its grid until macOS Ventura replaced it with System Settings and a scrolling sidebar modelled on the iPhone.

Today the pattern is nearly universal: a sidebar of sections on the left, a search field at the top and a detail pane on the right. Windows 11, macOS, ChromeOS and recent GNOME releases all use it, and iOS runs the phone-sized version of the same idea.

Search is what makes the pattern survivable. iOS added a search field to Settings in iOS 9, and every desktop system now indexes setting names, so typing bluetooth or caption skips the hierarchy entirely. It also quietly compensates for the fact that almost nobody remembers where things live any more.

The trade-off is that search only finds what you can name. If a feature was renamed in the version you are running, the old term returns nothing and the setting looks as though it was removed, which is the single most common cause of a support call about a missing option.

body.h2: Why sections keep splitting and getting renamed
body.html:
Sections split for three reasons. Features multiply, so one wireless entry becomes a network group with sub-pages. Permissions become per-app, so a single privacy switch becomes a list of dozens of apps. And new disclosure screens need somewhere to sit.

Renaming usually follows a change of scope. Apple widened Privacy to Privacy and Security in iOS 16, Windows 11 replaced Ease of Access with Accessibility to match industry wording, and GNOME retired Universal Access for the same reason. Android's Oreo restructure folded many top-level entries into a shorter grouped list, and manufacturer skins then reorganise them again.

body.h2: Tracking the changes version by version
body.html:
None of that helps when a support article describes one path and the screen shows another. The practical fix is to compare versions directly instead of trusting memory. The version change log records what moved between releases, and the settings finder resolves a feature name to its path on a specific version.

To see the two desktop lineages next to each other, macOS compared with Windows covers the current layouts. The osimulator settings browser opens 87 version combinations, old grids included, in a browser tab with nothing to install.

faq.q: Is Control Panel gone in Windows 11?
faq.a: No. Control Panel still ships with Windows 11 and some legacy dialogs open it, although Microsoft keeps moving individual applets into the Settings app.

faq.q: Why did System Preferences become System Settings?
faq.a: macOS Ventura replaced the icon grid with a sidebar list that mirrors iOS and iPadOS, and the name changed to match Apple's other platforms.

faq.q: Why do menu paths in older tutorials fail?
faq.a: Sections get renamed or split when features grow. Compare the version you are running against the one the tutorial was written for before assuming a setting was removed.

key: Grids gave way to sidebars once features outgrew a single screen
Windows ran two settings apps in parallel for over a decade
Search now compensates for constant renaming and splitting

title: Teach Device Skills with an OS Settings Simulator in Class
h1: Teaching device skills with a settings simulator
desc: Teach device skills with a simulator in classrooms and helpdesk training: safe practice, repeatable walkthroughs and clean screenshots for your support docs.
lede: Teaching someone to find a setting usually means putting the right device in their hands, on the right version, and accepting that they might change something. A browser-based settings simulator removes all three problems at once.

body.h2: Why a simulator beats a spare device
body.html:
Hardware is the first obstacle in any device training session. A classroom rarely has an iPhone, an Android phone, a Windows laptop and a Chromebook per learner, and borrowing personal devices means real settings get changed by accident.

A simulator has none of those costs. Nothing is installed, no account is created and no real configuration is touched, so thirty learners can each open a different system at the same time. It also fixes the version problem, because you can show the release a learner actually has instead of the one on your own phone.

In teaching, the value is repeatability. Every learner sees the same menu tree, so an instruction such as open the network section and find the saved networks list produces the same screen for everyone, and a wrong turn costs one click.

That also makes assessment straightforward. Ask learners to describe the path they took in words, rather than to hand over a device, and you can check the answer against the same menu tree they used.

Digital literacy courses can build tasks around ordinary chores: joining a network, enlarging text, or checking for an update. The Wi-Fi guide and the software update guide work well as worksheets because they name the section rather than assuming a single layout.

Helpdesk training has a different problem: agents support systems they do not personally use. One agent may take calls about iPhones, Android phones and Chromebooks in a single shift, and reading a knowledge base article is a poor substitute for seeing the menu.

Simulated menus let new agents rehearse the twenty most common call reasons before they speak to anyone. Pair the practice with the guide library for the written path, and keep the settings finder open during live calls, for when a caller describes a feature but cannot say where it lives.

Documentation is the third use. Screenshots taken from a real device carry personal data: account names, phone numbers, network names and email addresses all have to be blurred before publishing, and blurred screenshots read badly.

Screens captured from a simulator are already clean, consistent in size and easy to retake when a version changes. If you maintain documentation for several platforms, the operating system index shows which systems and versions you can capture. Retaking a set of screenshots after an operating system update becomes a short task rather than a hunt for the right hardware, which is usually what stops documentation from being kept current. And the comparison pages help when one article has to cover two platforms at once.

Set expectations honestly with learners. A simulator reproduces menu structure, not device state. Toggles you flip change nothing, and sample values such as device names, build numbers and network details are illustrative rather than live readings. The data provenance page sets out which parts are taken verbatim from open-source code and which are placeholders.

That limit is acceptable for teaching navigation, which is where most support calls stall anyway. Open the osimulator settings simulator and build your first walkthrough around a task your learners already ask about.

faq.q: Can learners break anything in a simulator?
faq.a: No. The menus are a reproduction of structure, so nothing they change affects a real device or any account.

faq.q: Does it work on school networks without installs?
faq.a: It runs in a browser tab with no download and no sign-in, so it works on managed machines where software installation is blocked.

faq.q: Can I use the screenshots in internal documentation?
faq.a: Yes, and they are cleaner than device captures because they contain no personal names, numbers or network details to redact.

Simulator screenshots need no blurring before publishing
Teach navigation with it; device state still needs real hardware

title: Try iOS Online: Explore Android and 40+ Systems in a Browser
h1: Try iOS and Android online, without owning either device
desc: Try iOS online alongside Android and 40 more systems in your browser, with no download, and learn exactly what a settings simulator can and cannot show you.
lede: You can open the settings menus of iOS, Android and more than forty other systems in a browser tab, with nothing to install. Knowing precisely where the reproduction stops is what makes it useful rather than misleading.

body.h2: What you get in a browser tab
body.html:
Wanting to see how the other platform works is a common reason to borrow somebody's phone. A settings simulator answers the same question in a tab: you open iOS, iPadOS, Android, Windows, macOS, Ubuntu, ChromeOS or any of more than forty systems and move through the menus the way you would on the hardware.

There is no download, no account and no virtual machine waiting to boot. Because it runs in the page rather than streaming a device, it also works on managed or locked-down computers where installing software is not permitted.

That makes it a practical way to settle an argument about which platform buries a feature deeper, to prepare for a switch, or to follow instructions written for a device you do not have in front of you.

The simulator reproduces menu structure: the sections, the order they appear in, the sub-pages behind each row and the wording of the labels. For Android, Ubuntu, ChromeOS, webOS OSE and Firefox OS that structure is machine-extracted verbatim from the systems' open-source code rather than retyped from screenshots, so the labels match the source.

It also spans 87 version combinations, which matters because sections move between releases. Opening two versions of the same system side by side shows what was renamed, and the version change log lists those differences in writing.

Be equally clear about the other half. A simulator cannot show live device state, and it does not claim to. The sample values on screen, including device names, IP addresses, serial and build numbers, storage figures and the position of individual switches, are illustrative placeholders rather than readings taken from a real machine.

So never quote a build number or a network address from the simulator as fact, and do not expect a toggle to reflect how any particular phone is configured. The data provenance page states item by item which parts come verbatim from source and which are sample data.

Inside that boundary it handles a large share of everyday questions, because most of them are about navigation rather than state. Where does the eSIM section sit on this Android version. Which screen holds the update button. What is this option called now that it has been renamed.

Walk the path once, then send the person a written version. Pairing the walk with a guide keeps the wording consistent: the eSIM guide and the screenshot guide both name sections rather than assuming one layout, and the settings finder maps a feature name to its path.

If you are considering a switch, open the system you do not own and read its first three sections. Those hold the settings you touch weekly, and the differences in naming show up immediately. Battery, storage and notification controls are the usual sticking points, and seeing them once removes most of the friction of moving across.

iOS compared with Android is a useful companion for the mobile pair, and the iOS hub lists which releases you can open. Then load the osimulator settings simulator and pick a system you have never used at all.

faq.a: No. It is a faithful reproduction of the settings menus, not an emulated device, so apps do not run and nothing on screen reflects real hardware.

faq.q: Are the values shown in the menus real?
faq.a: No. Device names, IP addresses, build numbers and switch positions are illustrative sample values, as the data provenance page explains in detail.

faq.a: Neither. It opens in a browser tab, runs offline once loaded, and asks for no sign-in.
